extracted.intended_audience: aspiring courtiers, statesmen, and individuals seeking to advance their fortune in public or political life
extracted.subtask_description: Practical precepts for individuals seeking to advance their personal fortune and position in public life: how to gather information, judge and present oneself, choose friends and competitors, adapt to occasions, and order means (mind, wealth, reputation, honour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer discourse grounded in full histories/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form for instruction about negotiation and government is discourse upon histories or examples rather than abstract aphorisms; particulars drawn freshly from history show circumstances and supply patterns for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples set down at large include attendant circumstances which can control or supply the discourse; succinctly cited examples lack particularity and appear servile to the discourse. (Contrast fables/aphorisms and prefer living, circumstantial histories.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lives and letters for business particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: For discourse about private business and conduct, histories of lives are most popular; even better for particulars are weighty letters (e.g., Cicero ad Atticum), which represent business more particularly than chronicles or lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking concrete guidance about personal affairs prefer letters and lives that reveal private actions and motives rather than broad chronicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish wisdom of counsel vs wisdom for one’s own fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a wisdom of counsel (public/statecraft) and a wisdom for pressing one’s own fortune; they sometimes meet but often differ — being clever for oneself may be hurtful for government and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the different aims: counsel aims at the circumference (public ends), private wisdom at the centre (personal advantage). Examples: ants (wise for themselves but harmful to garden). Adjust conduct according to which wisdom is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute success prudently—avoid arrogant self-credit
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impolitic and unlucky to openly ascribe all success to one’s own skill; great politiques attributed successes to felicity rather than skill (e.g., Timotheus’s repeated disclaimers and subsequent ill fortune).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly ascribe successes to fortune/felicity rather than boastful claims of sole skill; boastful professions invite misfortune and resentment (examples: Timotheus, Pharaoh quotations). Sylla styled himself Felix, not Magnus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use maxims of fortune as spur, not as pretext for insolency
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxims suggesting one can make his fortune (Faber quisque fortunæ suæ) are valuable as spurs to industry if used modestly, but dangerous if turned into presumption and outward declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt such beliefs privately to motivate action, but avoid public arrogance that provokes displeasure; keep them as internal resolution rather than public stirrups to insolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain good, particular information about persons and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Procure detailed information about persons (natures, desires, ends, customs, helps, weaknesses, friends, factions, dependences) and of actions (what’s on foot, how conducted, favoured or opposed) — particulars are the minor propositions in active syllogisms and crucial for correct conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information must be specific and timely; without accurate particulars even excellent general observations yield error. Treat such information as a main independent part of political knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice slowness of belief and distrust; prefer deeds/countenance to words
rubrics_metrics.description: The sinews of wisdom include slowness to believe and a disposition to distrust; give more credit to countenances and deeds than to words, and within words value surprised/sudden passages over set/put speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study subtle motions of countenance (Animi janua) and sudden slips of speech; be wary of commanded or practiced countenances. Examples: Tiberius/Gallus and Tacitus’ readings of gestures and style of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge deeds by magnitude and nature — beware of small favours
rubrics_metrics.description: Deeds are not always trustworthy without considering their magnitude and nature: small favours often lull caution and industry and may be designed to deceive (Fraus sibi in parvis...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat trivial rewards skeptically; small benefits can be bait to larger betrayals. Example: Mutianus’s hollow reconcilement of Antonius Primus where small favors masked a strategic desolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words strategically: emotions reveal truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, though full of flattery and uncertainty, can reveal truth when passion or incitement elicits hidden sentiments; counter-dissimulation can draw out truths (tell a lie and you may find a truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not wholly despise verbal testimony; provoke or create conditions (anger, kindness, bravery) where concealed sentiment surfaces. Example: Tiberius’s retort to Agrippina revealing inward thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek reports from varied sources: enemies, friends, servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-hand knowledge is most sound when gathered from those closest to the person: enemies reveal weaknesses, friends virtues and abilities, servants customs and times, familiar friends reveal conceits and opinions; general fame is light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor domestic or immediate sources ('verior fama e domesticis emanat') over public reputations; triangulate reports across sources for a fuller picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret people by natures and ends, noting predominancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are best disclosed by their natures and ends: weaker men by their natures, wiser by their ends. For princes, nature often better interprets because they have few particular ends; for private persons, ends are more telling. Also determine which humour or end predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-attributing complex ends where simple nature will explain behavior; assess whether a person’s dominant humour or interest will guide most decisions (example: Tigellinus exploiting Nero’s fears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three compounded ways to inquire effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: The most compendious methods: (1) have acquaintance with those who look most into the world and one well-informed friend per business kind; (2) keep a mediocrity in liberty of speech and secrecy — liberty to elicit speech, secrecy to induce trust; (3) habitually observe and make it a practice to learn in every conference and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance openness (to invite information) and secrecy (to secure trust); cultivate a few well-placed informants and a watchful, learning disposition (Et hoc volo, et etiam aliquid addiscere). Beware that knowing much does not lead to rash meddling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know thyself impartially — inventory abilities and lacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Take an impartial view of one’s abilities and impediments; account faults with weight and virtues with moderation to form practical considerations about life and choice of course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'politic glass' (state of the world) to see oneself; avoid self-delusion by regularly reassessing fit with the times, profession, competitors, and means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how your nature fits the times
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether your constitution of nature suits the general state of the times; if concordant give yourself more scope, if dissonant be retired and reserved (e.g., Tiberius vs Augustus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify public exposure based on historical moment: some times reward conspicuousness, others secrecy. Use this to decide engagement level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a profession suited to your nature and change if free
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how your nature matches professions and courses of life; if free, choose accordingly; if already engaged, depart at first opportunity when misfit is clear (Duke Valentine example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid remaining in roles ill-suited to your disposition, because misalignment reduces chance of eminence and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select arenas with fewer competitors to maximize eminence
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how you sort with likely competitors and choose paths where you can be most solitary and eminent (Cæsar left oratory because Cicero/Hortensius dominated and turned to martial greatness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the competitive landscape and seek niches where your natural strengths make you stand out rather than be eclipsed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose friends and dependents according to your nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Form friendships and retinues composed of those complementary to your natural disposition and aims (Cæsar’s followers were active and effectual, not solemn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate dependents who help carry out your chosen mode of action; mismatch between leader and followers undermines effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware imitation: do not assume you can do as another did
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious in thinking you can replicate others’ successes; differences in nature and carriage mean that what worked for one (e.g., Sylla) may not work for another (Pompey’s failure to replicate Sylla).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the fit between your qualities and the example’s qualities before copying; avoid overconfidence ('Sylla potuit, ego non potero' error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal and set forth oneself artfully and sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: There is advantage in setting forth one’s virtues, fortunes, merits and in artfully covering weaknesses — but ostentation requires art to avoid turning tedious or arrogant and is morally a vice but politically useful within limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasteful ostentation: mix with perilous contexts, envied moments, or easy transitions to and from it; balance self-praise with self-deprecation occasionally to avoid disgust. Excessive ostentation repels the wise but convinces many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid devaluing virtue by overexposure or haste
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue can be debased by (1) obtruding oneself to be accepted, (2) doing too much causing satiety, (3) finding fruit of virtue too soon and being pleased with little — these reduce the real worth and long-term benefit of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid premature display, excessive output without pause, and early satisfactions; let virtues settle and be appreciated over time (Cave ne insuetus rebus maioribus videaris).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover defects by caution, colour, or confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Three methods to conceal or mitigate defects: (a) caution — avoid situations unsuited to you; (b) colour — provide plausible explanations why faults arise from better causes; (c) confidence — despise what you cannot attain, or boldly affect mastery over weak points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate remedial technique: avoid playing to weaknesses when possible, reframe limits as virtues, or face them confidently. Beware showing too much meekness, which invites scorn; show sparks of spirit to protect against contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the mind pliant and obedient to occasion (versatility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the mind to be flexible and ready to change with occasions; fixedness and inability to depart from one’s habitual course is highly prejudicial to fortune (Idem manebat...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate versatile judgment and readiness to alter conduct when conditions change; avoid attachment to methods that once succeeded (Fabius Maximus example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Run with occasions but choose passable courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not only turn with occasions; run with them but avoid straining credit or strength to over-hard points — choose actions that are most passable to preserve reputation and future options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer moderate, widely palatable actions that avoid overcommitment; this preserves capacity and builds sustained reputation and felicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine opportunism with plotting — both capacities required
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of sufficiency: one adept at using occasions dexterously, another at plotting and pursuing designs; both are imperfect without the other and a complete politician needs both capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop both tactical adaptability and strategic plotting abilities; failing in either limits effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate secrecy and disclosure—over-dissimulating is weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth of secrecy can be admirable, but continual dissimulation breeds error and can entrap the dissimulator; greatest politiques sometimes profess desires rather than endlessly disguise them (examples: Sylla, Cæsar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use secrecy where it imports and publicity where it aids aims; avoid a permanent habit of deep dissimulation which is tactically limited and morally inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge proportions and values, not mere show
rubrics_metrics.description: Accustom your mind to judge proportionally what conduces to your ends; many err by valuing show (access to princes, applause) over substance and effect, or by equating labor with meaningful gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer things that materially advance ends over those that appear costly or impressive; measure by fit and effect rather than apparent effort or ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marshal pursuits in right order: mind, means, reputation, honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize pursuits: first amend the mind (remove impediments), second obtain means/wealth, third secure reputation (hard to regain), and lastly honour (more easily won by other goods). Also respect temporal order — do what is now fitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing great ends before necessary beginnings; act in the order of time and practicality (Quod nunc instat agamus). Solon/Crœsus example: material means less decisive than quality of men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engagements that consume excessive time to the detriment of opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not embrace matters that occupy too much time (e.g., certain learned professions) if they prevent learning particulars, awaiting occasions, or devising plots essential for advancing fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance professional obligations with time to gather information and pursue opportunistic actions; long, consuming careers reduce flexibility and chance for fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate nature: interlace business and seek secondary outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Act so that every action has subsidiary uses: if you cannot obtain your primary aim, secure a second or third benefit; make failures into seeds for future gain or respectable opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never put all hopes into a single line; integrate multiple possible outcomes into each action and extract any available gain (win some good opinion, seed future projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Always keep an exit or retreat — avoid peremptory commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage peremptorily without a ‘window to fly out at’; always preserve a way to retire should circumstances change (two frogs parable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan contingencies and escape routes; avoid irreversible commitments that trap you after conditions shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate attachments and friendships—avoid over-embarcation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt Bias’s counsel modestly: love as if a future enemy, hate as if to be loved — avoid embarking too far into unfortunate friendships, spleens, envies, or emulations which betray utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep emotional and social ties measured to preserve independence and prevent irreparable costs from misjudged attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject evil arts despite expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: While corrupt Machiavellian arts (seeking appearance of virtue only, ruling by fear, sowing internal thorns, setting states aflame to fish in troubled waters) can more quickly press a man’s fortune, they are foul and short ways are often unclean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fairer, more durable paths even if slower; the shortest path to fortune is commonly the foulest. Moral and reputational costs make such arts undesirable despite occasional short-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep moral perspective: well-being, virtue, and their rewards/punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep before your eyes that being without well-being is a curse, and that generally virtue is its own reward and vice punished: moral considerations temper pursuit of fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance political prudence with ethical reflection; understand that some men forgo fortune for higher respects, and that long-term felicity is tied to virtue as much as to manipulation.
